body: Bitcoin fell for a third consecutive day, according to CoinDesk, as a slide in Asian technology shares added to the gloom hanging over crypto markets.

The standout detail came from BlackRock's spot bitcoin exchange-traded fund. CoinDesk reports it logged its largest single-day outflow since it launched more than two years ago, a sign that investors are continuing to pull money out of the sector.

The material available gives no price levels, outflow figures or other specifics, so the exact size of the move is not something we can put a number on here. What is clear is the direction: down for bitcoin, down for Asian tech, and out the door for ETF money.

The link between the two markets is worth noting. Bitcoin has often traded like a risk asset, moving in step with growth and technology stocks when investors turn cautious. When tech shares stumble, crypto frequently feels the tremor, and that pattern appears to be playing out again.

The ETF angle matters because spot bitcoin funds were meant to be the sturdy bridge between traditional finance and crypto. A record outflow from the biggest name in that category suggests that the bridge can carry traffic in both directions, and right now people are heading for the exit.

Whether this is a short-term shakeout or the start of something longer will depend on whether the selling continues and what happens in broader tech markets. For now, three red days and a record redemption make for a rough week in crypto.
bef66a471b57.summary: Bitcoin fell for a third straight day as Asian tech shares slid, while BlackRock's spot bitcoin ETF saw its biggest single-day outflow since launching over two years ago, CoinDesk reports.
bef66a471b57.pixel_take: Bitcoin has now had three bad days in a row, and BlackRock's ETF just set a record for people leaving the party. Nobody is even pretending to look for their coat quietly.
bef66a471b57.why_it_matters: Record outflows from the largest spot bitcoin ETF show institutional-style money can leave as fast as it arrived. Bitcoin's tendency to move with tech stocks means weakness in equities can spill straight into crypto holdings and portfolios.
key_points: Bitcoin fell for a third straight day, per CoinDesk.
BlackRock's spot bitcoin ETF had its largest single-day outflow since launch over two years ago.
Asian tech shares also slid, adding pressure on risk assets.

4fa85ae7ae72.headline: Trump Threatens Ban on US Firms Building AI Data Centres Abroad, Surprising Even His Own Team
body: President Donald Trump said he will bar American companies from building AI data centres outside the United States, threatening a "tremendous tax" on tech firms that try. He made the remarks to reporters at a press briefing after returning from a trip to Asia, according to BBC News.

Details were thin. Trump said members of his own team were hearing about the idea for the first time, and it is unclear how such a policy would be enforced. His stated reason was competition with China, which he said would "take all of them" if US firms built abroad.

The comments land in a crowded week for tech policy. On Monday, Washington announced that firms would need a licence to buy advanced computer chips, so officials can check whether the hardware is serving Chinese companies or being smuggled into China. That move is expected to hit South East Asian countries that have invested heavily in data centres, where Chinese firms look to rent computing power.

Big tech has already been spreading its bets. Meta has broken ground on a data centre in Alberta, Canada, and Anthropic has signed a long-term lease deal for a proposed site in Nova Scotia. Google announced a €13bn investment in AI infrastructure in Finland in September; building work on two of its three centres there was halted last month over forest clearance concerns. Trump singled out Finland, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen".

Politics at home is part of the backdrop. Data centres were a major issue in the 3 November midterms, with Democratic candidates promising tougher rules over noise and energy use, and several winning. Pew Research Centre figures cited by the BBC put the US at about 3,000 data centres as of April, with 1,500 more in the pipeline. Trump urged local communities to welcome them and make operators pay.
4fa85ae7ae72.summary: Trump says he will ban US firms from building AI data centres overseas and tax those that do, but gave few details. The idea would hit plans by Meta, Google and others abroad.
4fa85ae7ae72.pixel_take: Announcing a sweeping policy and then telling your team 'they're here, I'm telling them now' is certainly one way to run a cabinet meeting. Somewhere, a Finnish forest is wondering what all the fuss is.
4fa85ae7ae72.why_it_matters: AI infrastructure is among the biggest spending areas in tech, and a ban or tax on overseas builds could upend multibillion-dollar plans and raise costs for the firms involved. Combined with new chip licensing rules, it signals tighter government control over where AI computing power lives, which matters for tech stocks and investors.
key_points: Trump says he will ban US firms from building AI data centres abroad and threatens a heavy tax, with no details given.
The idea follows new chip licensing rules aimed at stopping advanced chips from serving Chinese firms.
Meta, Google and Anthropic have overseas data centre projects that could be affected.

07194b192617.headline: Too big to watch? A TechCrunch writer's 65-inch OLED upgrade came with a side of nausea
body: A TechCrunch writer who traded a long-serving 55-inch TCL smart TV for a 65-inch LG evo C4 OLED, the company's mid-range 2024 model, reports that the upgrade brought some unexpected side effects, according to the outlet's recent first-person piece.

The picture was everything cinephiles promise. OLED screens use self-lit pixels rather than an LED backlight shining through a panel, which allows finer control and deeper colors and shadows. The writer dove into a collection of 4K Blu-rays, until midway through "McCabe and Mrs. Miller" a wave of nausea hit. It lasted several hours and was followed by a mild tension headache.

The writer found they are not alone. Reddit is full of new OLED owners describing similar queasiness, and one even reported feeling sick a day after buying an LG C2. Another said their wife felt sick watching an 85-inch set. There is no consensus on the cause: motion smoothing, sitting too close and screen brightness all get blamed.

None of those fit the writer's case. Motion smoothing was off, the seat was nine feet away (within the recommended range for 65 inches), and brightness was turned down to about 50 percent. The writer's own theory is that their eyes simply had to learn to take in a much bigger picture, a bit like staring at something out a moving car's window. After a few days, the nausea went away.

The piece also flags practical issues. The wide screen ships detached from its base, is hard to move without help, and comes without detailed assembly instructions, so a YouTube tutorial and careful handling are advised. Buyers should also check that a room can handle a set this size. The verdict: the C4 is spectacular, with a short learning curve.
07194b192617.summary: A TechCrunch writer's jump to a 65-inch LG C4 OLED brought stunning visuals and a bout of nausea that faded after a few days. Setup and room size are also worth considering before buying.
07194b192617.pixel_take: Your new TV is so good your eyes need a few days of orientation, like a new hire who got a corner office with a cinema screen.
07194b192617.why_it_matters: OLED sets cost significantly more than LED models, so buyers are spending real money on a bigger, better screen. Knowing that adjustment, room size and setup can bite helps avoid a costly return or a disappointing purchase.
key_points: The writer upgraded from a 55-inch TCL to a 65-inch LG evo C4 OLED.
Nausea and a headache hit during a movie, a reported common experience among new OLED owners, and faded within days.
The set ships detached from its base without detailed instructions, and room size matters.

699ea053e18a.headline: Flanagan Tips Her Hat to Schumer, Then Swoons Over Van Hollen's 'Organizer' Style
body: Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.) said on Sunday that she appreciates Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer's leadership and his work in the upper chamber, according to The Hill. In the same breath, she praised Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) and his bid for a leadership role.

Flanagan said Van Hollen leads "like an organizer," which is a compliment with a pointed subtext. The teaser we have is cut off after that phrase, so the full detail of her comparison is not available. What is clear is the structure: a polite nod to the incumbent, then real enthusiasm for the challenger.

The framing is classic Senate diplomacy. Praising a leader's service while promoting an alternative lets a newcomer signal where she stands without declaring open war on the person who may control committee assignments and floor strategy. It is the political equivalent of saying the old restaurant was lovely, then handing out coupons for the new place.

Based on the material provided, Van Hollen is seeking leadership and Flanagan is a senator-elect who has already weighed in. We do not have details on how many colleagues back him, when any vote might happen, or what exactly the role would be, so those questions remain open.

Even so, public comments from incoming senators matter. Leadership contests inside a party are usually decided by a small group of colleagues, and every early endorsement or warm word can shape momentum before the ballots are cast.
699ea053e18a.summary: Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan said she appreciates Chuck Schumer's leadership but praised Chris Van Hollen's bid for leadership, saying he leads "like an organizer," according to The Hill.
699ea053e18a.pixel_take: Flanagan thanked Schumer politely and then gushed about Van Hollen. In Washington, that's the "it's not you, it's... well, actually, maybe it's a little you" speech.
699ea053e18a.why_it_matters: Senate Democratic leadership shapes legislative strategy, judicial confirmations and how the party negotiates on spending and taxes, all of which can move markets and affect household budgets. A shift in leadership could change how aggressively the party pursues its agenda.
key_points: Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan said she appreciates Chuck Schumer's leadership.
She praised Chris Van Hollen's leadership bid, saying he leads "like an organizer."
Details on vote timing and support were not in the available material.

13e2c07ae4a3.headline: Apple Intelligence on iOS 27 can eat up to 14GB of iPhone storage, and turning it off isn't enough
body: Apple Intelligence has grown up with iOS 27, and so has its appetite. According to Engadget, Apple says the features need up to 14GB on the iPhone Duo, iPhone Air and iPhone 17 Pro or later, and 8GB on all other compatible iPhones.

Real-world numbers may be messier. Some users have reported the features occupying anywhere from 9GB to 16GB. On a 128GB phone, that is more than 12 percent of the total space going to tools you may never touch.

The catch is that switching the features off no longer frees the space. Engadget reports that iOS 27 keeps the files around in case you change your mind. There is no single toggle that makes them vanish the way there once was.

The workaround relies on a quirk: Apple Intelligence only runs when the device language and the Siri language match. Set Siri to a different language while leaving the iPhone's language alone, restart, and the storage should come back. Engadget cautions that this is a workaround and a future update could break it.

If you want some AI features but not others, you can toggle individual tools, though that is unlikely to save noticeable space. Users have reported that iOS deletes unused Apple Intelligence files on its own when storage runs critically low.

What you give up is not trivial. The revamped Siri now understands context, acts inside other apps and can find details like hotel reservations or flight numbers. There is also a Siri mode in the camera, better photo cleanup, tab sorting by topic in Safari, natural-language Shortcuts and automatic proofreading. As Engadget puts it, the choice comes down to space versus convenience.
13e2c07ae4a3.summary: Apple Intelligence in iOS 27 needs up to 14GB on some iPhones, and disabling it doesn't free that space. Engadget describes a Siri-language workaround to reclaim storage, at the cost of the new AI features.
13e2c07ae4a3.pixel_take: Your phone's new brain weighs up to 14GB, and it refuses to move out even after you tell it to stop living there. Classic roommate behavior.
13e2c07ae4a3.why_it_matters: Storage is a real cost for buyers, since larger-capacity iPhones cost more, and AI features that claim gigabytes quietly shift that math. It also shows how on-device AI trades local resources for convenience, a tension every phone maker will face.
key_points: Apple says Apple Intelligence needs up to 14GB on newer iPhones and 8GB on other compatible models.
Turning the features off doesn't delete them; mismatching Siri and device languages reclaims the space.
The workaround may break in future updates, and you lose the new Siri and other AI tools.

665b02d8d90f.headline: U.S. Midterms and Your Portfolio: What Investors Are Asking
body: Investing.com has published a piece asking what the U.S. midterm elections mean for investors. The full text wasn't available to us, so we can't report its specific arguments or forecasts, and we won't pretend otherwise.

What we can do is offer well-established context. Midterm elections decide control of Congress, and that shapes how easily a sitting president can pass tax changes, spending bills and regulation. Markets tend to care less about who wins than about whether the result produces gridlock or a clear path for policy.

A divided Congress is often read by investors as a sign that big, disruptive legislation is less likely. Some see that as calming, since fewer surprises can mean easier planning for companies. Others worry about standoffs over government funding or the debt ceiling.

Sectors can feel the effects differently. Policy on energy, healthcare, financials and technology is often debated around elections, and investors sometimes reposition ahead of expected changes. But election-driven moves are frequently overtaken by interest rates, inflation and corporate earnings.

For everyday investors, the usual advice is to avoid making big portfolio swings based on political guesses alone. Diversification and a long-term plan have historically done more work than trying to time the ballot box.
665b02d8d90f.summary: Investing.com asks what the U.S. midterms mean for investors. Without the full text, here is general context on how congressional control, gridlock and policy expectations can influence markets.
665b02d8d90f.pixel_take: Investors want to know what the midterms mean for markets. Short answer from history: don't bet the portfolio on a ballot, because the market has its own opinions and they rarely come with a campaign slogan.
665b02d8d90f.why_it_matters: Congressional control shapes taxes, spending and regulation, all of which can influence corporate profits and sector performance. Understanding that elections are only one driver among many, alongside rates and earnings, can help investors avoid costly knee-jerk moves with their money.
key_points: Investing.com posed the question of what the U.S. midterms mean for investors.
Midterms decide congressional control, which affects tax, spending and regulatory policy.
Long-term planning and diversification usually matter more than election timing.

50a5a499604d.headline: IMF chief warns AI boom will keep interest rates climbing: 'You snooze, you lose'
body: Kristalina Georgieva, managing director of the International Monetary Fund, warned at the 2026 Apec summit in Shenzhen that booming demand for artificial intelligence will push the world's major central banks toward higher interest rates, according to The Guardian.

Her logic is simple. Demand for AI hardware and related tech products is lifting consumer prices worldwide, and it is stacking on top of the energy shock from the war in the Middle East. She said both factors would push global inflation to 4.7% this year. 'This calls for a tightening of monetary policy in many economies,' she said.

Central banks are already in hiking mode. The war that began in February sent oil above $100 a barrel, and the European Central Bank raised rates in June for the first time since 2023. The US Federal Reserve followed in September and the Bank of England earlier this month. Markets expect more increases next year. Oil has recently eased after the US midterms and a pickup in crude supply.

Georgieva argued the two shocks differ in staying power: the energy hit should eventually fade, but 'AI is forever'. AI hardware and related products now make up more than a tenth of world goods trade, and that share is climbing fast. Some countries are reaping far more of the investment than others, hence her warning that countries need digital infrastructure, AI-ready workers and safeguards against financial stability and cybersecurity risks.

The caution comes with plenty of froth around it. A day earlier the ECB flagged growing debt taken on by AI companies, drawing 'historic parallels' with the dotcom bubble and the sub-prime crisis. Yet Anthropic, maker of the Claude chatbot, debuted on the US stock market on Thursday, pricing at $83 per share in the largest IPO proceeds on record, per the Guardian. It is expected to be valued around $1.5tn despite $80bn in losses in the first half of 2026.
50a5a499604d.summary: IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva says AI-driven demand and the Middle East energy shock will push global inflation to 4.7% and require tighter monetary policy, even as the ECB warns of AI debt risks.
50a5a499604d.pixel_take: The AI boom is so hot that central banks now have to hold the ice bucket. Meanwhile Anthropic's IPO suggests investors packed swimwear.
50a5a499604d.why_it_matters: If AI demand keeps inflation high, borrowing costs for mortgages, loans and businesses may stay elevated longer than hoped. Investors also face a double risk: tighter policy and an AI sector that regulators compare to past bubbles.
key_points: IMF's Georgieva says AI demand plus the energy shock will lift global inflation to 4.7% this year and calls for tighter policy.
The ECB, Fed and Bank of England have already raised rates, and markets expect more hikes next year.
The ECB warns AI-company debt echoes the dotcom and sub-prime bubbles, even as Anthropic's IPO aims for a $1.5tn valuation.

0985b71f3d0a.headline: Chainflip confirms $12M hack, dangles 10% bounty to get the loot back
body: Chainflip has confirmed it suffered a hack worth about $12 million, and it is now trying to negotiate rather than just fume. According to Cointelegraph, the project has offered the attacker a 10% bounty if the rest of the stolen funds come back by Nov. 23.

The terms, as described in the report, are simple: return 90% of the stolen money, keep the other 10%, and Chainflip will treat the whole episode as a white-hat recovery. The project also promised to withdraw any law enforcement complaints if the deal is honored.

That kind of offer is a familiar move in crypto. When stolen funds sit on a public blockchain, they are hard to spend quietly, and tracing them is often easier than cashing them out. Projects know that chasing a hacker through courts can be slow and uncertain, so a bounty can look like the faster way to recover most of the money.

The deadline adds pressure. A short window gives the attacker a clear choice between a negotiated exit with a payday and an open-ended game of cat and mouse. Whether the hacker bites is unknown, as the material available does not say how the attack happened or how the attacker has responded.

For users and traders, the key questions are how much of the loss is recovered and how any shortfall is handled. The teaser does not provide those details, so they remain open until Chainflip shares more.
0985b71f3d0a.summary: Chainflip confirmed a $12 million hack and offered the attacker a 10% bounty to return 90% of the funds by Nov. 23, promising to treat it as a white-hat recovery and drop law enforcement complaints.
0985b71f3d0a.pixel_take: Chainflip is basically telling the hacker: keep the tip, return the rest, and we'll pretend this was a very aggressive security audit. Customer service has never sounded so desperate.
0985b71f3d0a.why_it_matters: Hacks remain one of crypto's biggest risks, and every incident tests how much users can trust cross-chain and DeFi platforms with their money. Bounty deals can recover funds, but they also raise uncomfortable questions about rewarding attackers.
key_points: Chainflip confirmed a hack of about $12 million.
It offered a 10% bounty if 90% of funds are returned by Nov. 23.
The project promised to treat the return as white-hat and withdraw law enforcement complaints.

2ad0ceb8c2d3.headline: Settler Attacks Hit Three West Bank Villages as Violence Data Spikes and Israeli Politics Heats Up
body: Israeli settlers attacked several Palestinian towns and villages in the central occupied West Bank early on Sunday, burning 12 vehicles and spray-painting racist slogans on homes, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa as cited by Al Jazeera. Incidents were reported in Kafr Malik, Deir Abu Mash'al and Deir al-Sudan, in the Ramallah and el-Bireh areas.
Al Jazeera correspondent Nour Odeh, reporting from Kafr Malik, said residents woke around two in the morning to the sounds of fire and explosions and realised settlers had set cars alight.

The attack lands amid worrying numbers. The Palestinian Authority's Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission says 3,133 attacks were recorded in October, 1,764 by Israeli forces and 1,369 by settlers. That is a 53 percent rise from September's 2,051. Settler attacks alone climbed 112 percent, from 647 to 1,369. Al Jazeera also reports that at least 1,222 people, including 255 children, have been killed in attacks in the West Bank since October 2023.

The incident also became a political football. Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar Party and tasked with forming a new government after last month's election, called the attacks "Jewish terrorism" and blamed policies led by far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich for pushing the area toward anarchy. Ben-Gvir rejected the claims, said Eisenkot was jumping to conclusions, and accused him of paying a "down payment" to Arab Knesset member Ahmad Tibi ahead of a possible coalition.

Shai Parnes of the Israeli rights group B'Tselem told Al Jazeera that settlers are often escorted by Israeli forces who do nothing to stop them. The Israeli military said it was sending police and Criminal Identification Unit investigators to collect evidence as part of an ongoing investigation.
2ad0ceb8c2d3.summary: Settlers burned 12 vehicles and defaced homes in three West Bank villages, as Palestinian data shows settler attacks more than doubled in October and Israeli politicians trade blame.
2ad0ceb8c2d3.why_it_matters: Escalating West Bank violence adds to regional instability and shapes the diplomatic pressure Israel faces, which can affect risk perceptions in Middle East markets. The fight over responsibility could also influence coalition talks that determine Israel's next government and its policy direction.
key_points: Settlers burned 12 vehicles and sprayed racist slogans in Kafr Malik, Deir Abu Mash'al and Deir al-Sudan.
Palestinian commission says settler attacks rose 112 percent in October versus September.
Eisenkot called the attacks terrorism; Ben-Gvir rejected his accusations.

08360187a8fd.headline: Off-Broadway's 'Love Me' Hands Audiences Auracast Headphones to Make Them Hear Hearing Loss
body: At the 178-seat SoHo Playhouse in New York City, an off-Broadway show called Love Me gives every audience member wired headphones attached to a small Auracast receiver, according to The Verge. The one-man show, from comedian and former Saturday Night Live writer Drew Michael and director Prashanth Venkataramanujam, uses them as a core part of the storytelling.

Auracast is a Bluetooth-based technology that can broadcast high-quality audio to any number of nearby devices. Sound designer Daniel Kluger blends that stream with the theater's speakers. Tinnitus ringing and hearing-test tones slip into the music, and some sounds are muffled in the room and then dulled again by the headphones, so the audience gets a taste of what Michael hears.

One sound stays crisp: Michael's inner monologue, a mix of prerecorded tracks and his live microphone feed. Michael says the idea is that his inner world is the highest-fidelity space for him. In a stand-up club scene, three competing audio sources create deliberate overload, so viewers feel the effort of sorting out what is happening.

The payoff comes when audiograms from Michael's life appear on stage and the audience is told to take the headphones off. The show then moves into its final act, about Michael coming to understand his Deaf identity. He tells The Verge that deafness is not the problem, but the denial of it.

The production is presented with Deaf West Theatre. Beyond the audience feed, there is a separate Auracast channel built for hearing aids and cochlear implants, and iPads with captions are available. Michael performs with Auracast-enabled hearing aids that double as in-ear monitors, so he stays connected to the room. The reviewer notes any Auracast headphones can join the audience channel, and the Nothing Pro 1 connected in seconds.
Michael stresses the show is not really about gadgets. He argues that hearing technology and Deaf cultural identity should be a marriage rather than a divide.
08360187a8fd.summary: Love Me, an off-Broadway one-man show, uses Auracast headphones to put audiences inside Drew Michael's hearing loss, while also improving accessibility, according to The Verge.
08360187a8fd.pixel_take: Finally, a theater where telling people to put their headphones on is the plot, not a plea to stop them from texting.
08360187a8fd.why_it_matters: Auracast is moving from a spec-sheet feature to real-world use in venues, and this show suggests accessibility tech can also be a creative tool. As more earbuds, headphones and hearing aids support it, venues and device makers get a new market to serve.
key_points: Love Me gives each audience member an Auracast receiver and headphones at the SoHo Playhouse.
Separate Auracast channels serve hearing aid and cochlear implant users, with captioned iPads also available.
Any Auracast-capable headphones can join the audience broadcast, per The Verge's test.
